newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan backs down on U.S. attorney apology.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan backs down on U.S. attorney apology.

text.p: Pakistan said on Thursday a controversy over objectionable remarks about the country reported to have been made by a U.S. attorney must now end, apparently backing down on its demand for a public apology.

A Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters that enough had been said about the remarks by attorney Robert Horan in June, which sparked an outcry in Pakistan, and that "this matter can now be put to rest".
The apparent shift came only three days after the Foreign Ministry said it had called American ambassador Thomas Simons to tell him that an apology was still awaited from Horan.
He is reported to have made the remarks in connection with the arrest in June of a Pakistani, Mir Aimal Kansi, for a deadly shooting outside CIA headquarters in 1993.

Asked if the apology was no longer needed, the spokesman said: "We think that the U.S. officials, the State Department as well as the administration have already regretted (the remarks), they have dissociated themselves from these remarks, so I think...this matter should now be put to rest."

Pakistani newspapers quoted Horan as saying in a June 23 television interview that people in the region where Kansi lived were backward and could hand over their mothers for a far less amount than a $2 million U.S. award set for his arrest.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif called the reported remarks "uncivilised, irrational, unwarranted" and President Farooq Leghari said they "smell of racism".
On Thursday, the U.S. Information Service centre in Islamabad received a bomb threat by telephone, but it proved to be a hoax, police said.
The Foreign Ministry said on Monday the U.S. State Department had expressed sincere regrets and informed Islamabad that it had advised Horan to retract and issue a public apology.

Kansi, a native of the mainly tribal southwestern province of Baluchistan, bordering Afghanistan and Iran, was captured by agents of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation with the help of Pakistani commandos in an operation that sparked protests inside the country.
Some politicians accused Sharif of compromising national sovereignty by handing over a Pakistani to a foreign government without meeting legal formalities for extradition.

Islamabad has not explained its role in the capture of Kansi, the prime suspect for a shooting spree on January 25, 1993, outside the CIA's headquarters in Langley, Virginia, that killed two CIA workers and wounded three.
